Denver Real Estate Market Update: November 2026

Prices held steady in October, but fewer homes sold and most sellers helped with the buyer's costs. Buyers have room to negotiate right now.

By Chris Nowakiwsky, Broker Associate, RE/MAX ProfessionalsNovember 9, 2026

[CHRIS'S TAKE]

The Numbers

2,748homes sold in October, down 23.5% from a year ago
12,978active listings at month-end, up 3.9% from last October
65%of sales included a seller concession, averaging $12,557
30median days on market, down from 33 a year ago

Denver metro, October 2026. Source: DMAR Market Trends Report, October 2026 data.

Prices barely moved. The median single-family home in the metro sold for $645,000 in October, about the same as last year. Condos and townhomes sold for a median of $375,000, down about 3%.

What changed is how many homes are selling. Closings were down 23.5% from last October, and pending sales were down 20%, so I expect a slow December too. Inventory dipped from September, which is normal this time of year, but it's still higher than a year ago. Condos and townhomes have more than seven months of supply.

What I'm Seeing on the Ground

Homes are still selling for about 98% of list price. That number leaves out the concessions. Almost two out of three sellers in October paid something toward the buyer's closing costs or a rate buydown, and the average was $12,557.

In central Denver, I'm seeing more price reductions and more homes to choose from. Buyers are taking their time and looking for deals. With the average 30-year rate at 7.18% in early November (Freddie Mac), most buyers are focused on the monthly payment. A rate buydown can help them more than a small price cut.

Anyone selling right now needs a good reason to. The sellers I see doing well priced right from the start and knew what they were willing to give before the first showing.

The $1 Million-Plus Market

Homes over $1 million are still selling faster than the rest of the market. In October they sold in a median of 17 days, compared with 30 for the metro overall and 34 for $1 million-plus homes a year ago. They closed at about 98% of list price. Sales were down about 24% from last year, in line with the rest of the market.

Supply is about the same from $750,000 up to $2 million, roughly four months for single-family homes. Above $2 million it jumps to almost eight months. That's where buyers have the most leverage. In neighborhoods like Washington Park and Bonnie Brae, a well-priced home under $2 million still sells.

What It Means for Sellers

  • Expect to offer a concession. Most buyers are asking for help with closing costs or a rate buydown. Plan for it when you set your price.
  • Compare a buydown to a price cut. The same dollars toward a buyer's rate can lower their payment more than taking it off the price. I'll run both for you.
  • Price for today. With pending sales down 20%, an overpriced home will sit through the holidays. Your competition is what's for sale now, not what sold last spring.
  • If you can wait, get ready. Use the next two months for repairs, inspections and photos so you can list when buyers come back in January.

More in the seller guide, including a net proceeds calculator.

What It Means for Buyers

  • Ask for a concession. Most sellers are already giving one. Asking for help with closing costs or a rate buydown is normal right now.
  • Shop through the holidays. Fewer people tour homes between Thanksgiving and New Year's, and sellers still on the market usually need to move.
  • Look at homes that have been sitting. Condos and townhomes, and homes over $2 million, have the most supply and the most room to negotiate.
